claims.text: The target alloy is molten Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 prior to solidification.
A brief isothermal hold in the supercooled-liquid region after initial rapid cooling can suppress early nucleation.
Suppressing early nucleation through the hold will reduce primary crystallization.
The hold will enhance amorphous retention and thermal stability.
The proposed hold is applied slightly above the glass transition, after initial rapid cooling and before the final quench.
Melt spinning provides rapid cooling rates of approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s for this alloy.
A slower cooling condition of 52 K/s has been assessed for this alloy.
The 52 K/s condition was implemented on a copper plate.
The proposed hold is applicable to slower-cooling and subsequent reheating regimes in addition to rapid cooling.
Enhanced atomic diffusion and relaxation during the hold reduce the number and effectiveness of nucleation sites.
The hold permits homogenization and structural relaxation in the supercooled liquid.
Homogenization and structural relaxation lower the driving force for nucleation of primary non-eutectic phases and stabilize the amorphous structure during reheating.
Relative to no-hold samples, held samples will show fewer and less intense DSC crystallization exotherms.
Relative to no-hold samples, held samples will contain fewer crystalline phases by XRD and TEM.
Very rapid melt-spinning cooling produces an amorphous structure in this alloy.
Slow cooling produces a complex microstructure containing multiple crystalline phases.
The alloy undergoes extensive primary crystallization during reheating.
The hold should occur above the glass transition but before the onset of crystallization.
An FCC crystallization event occurs at approximately 1341 K under the cited faster-cooling condition.
Phosphorus and high mixing entropy promote glass formation during extremely rapid cooling of this alloy.

contradictions.description: The intervention is defined as occurring after an initial rapid-cooling step, whereas the conditions also present it as applicable to slower-cooling processing without explaining how the required initial rapid-cooling step would be incorporated.

The boundary labels approximately 1341 K as a 'rapid-cooling FCC crystallization temperature,' while the baseline states that rapid melt-spinning produces an amorphous structure. The evidence assigns 1341 K to accelerated cooling at 3018 K/s, not to the 10^5–10^6 K/s rapid-quenching condition.
